## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In the selected model of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]], let $H_\mu$ be the scalar one-particle Hilbert
space and let $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ be the
Dirac particle/antiparticle one-particle space. Let $\Omega_s$ and $\Omega_D$
be their zero-particle Fock vectors. The assignments of $H_\mu$ to bosonic
Fock space and $\mathcal K$ to CAR Fock space are the physical assumptions
of that postulate.

For every unit scalar wave-packet mode $h\in H_\mu$, define
$$|n\rangle_h=\frac{(a^\dagger(h))^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\Omega_s,\qquad n\ge0.$$
These vectors are normalized and mutually orthogonal, belong to the
finite-particle domain, and
$$a(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle_h,\qquad a^\dagger(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle_h,$$
where $a(h)|0\rangle_h=0$. The one-mode number operator
$N_h=a^\dagger(h)a(h)$ therefore satisfies
$N_h|n\rangle_h=n|n\rangle_h$. The maximal annihilation domain is the
square-summability domain of the sector images, as in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]].

For every unit Dirac particle mode $u\in\mathcal H_+$ or antiparticle mode
$u\in\overline{\mathcal H_-}$, regarded as a vector of $\mathcal K$, the
bounded operator $N_u=c^\dagger(u)c(u)$ is an orthogonal projection. The
one-mode subspace generated by $u$ is the closed span of
$\{(c^\dagger(u))^n\Omega_D:n\ge0\}$. It is spanned by $\Omega_D$ and
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$; the latter is normalized and
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. Thus a single Dirac CAR mode has occupation $0$ or $1$.
All statements are conditional on the adopted representations and
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. They do not derive which statistics nature assigns to
all fields and do not assert an experimental observation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The physical species assignments in [A1], Countable Choice in
[A2], and the mathematical Fock operator construction in [F1].

[A1] [[post-qft-free-field-model]] adopts the real scalar bosonic
symmetric-Fock model and the Dirac particle/antiparticle CAR-Fock model. This
is a physical model assumption, not a universal statistics theorem.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence of
nonempty sets has a choice function. The Fock supplier assumes this principle,
which is carried into this consumer.

[F1] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a separable
complex Hilbert space. It constructs the symmetric and antisymmetric Fock
spaces; the bosonic operators are mutual adjoints on their displayed domains
and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy
$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2 I$, while the fermionic operators
are bounded on the whole Fock space and satisfy
$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2 I$ and
$\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] gives the exact bosonic maximal domain
$D(a(h))=\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$.

[F3] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] defines each Fock vacuum as
$\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$, defines creation and annihilation by sector
insertion and contraction, and states $a(h)\Omega=c(h)\Omega=0$.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [A2], and [F1]–[F3]. All bosonic vectors constructed below lie in
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, so every displayed composition is defined.

1.1 Fix a unit $h\in H_\mu$ and put $v_n=(a^\dagger(h))^n\Omega_s$. The
vacuum relation is $a(h)\Omega_s=0$ and the CCR give
$a(h)a^\dagger(h)=a^\dagger(h)a(h)+I$. The base case is
$a(h)v_1=\Omega_s$. If $a(h)v_n=nv_{n-1}$, then
$a(h)v_{n+1}=a(h)a^\dagger(h)v_n
=a^\dagger(h)a(h)v_n+v_n
=n a^\dagger(h)v_{n-1}+v_n=(n+1)v_n$.
Thus $a(h)v_n=nv_{n-1}$ for every $n\ge1$. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Fix a unit $u\in\mathcal K$. By [F1],
$c(u)c^\dagger(u)+c^\dagger(u)c(u)=I$ and $c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. On
finite-particle vectors, the insertion and contraction formulas of [F3] give
$\langle c^\dagger(u)\xi,\eta\rangle_2=
\langle\xi,c(u)\eta\rangle_2$: the antisymmetric projection can be removed
against $\eta$, after which the tensor pairing contracts the inserted $u$
with the first factor. Since both operators are bounded by [F1] and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense by [F3], this identity extends to the whole
Fock space and gives $c^\dagger(u)=c(u)^*$. Also $c(u)\Omega_D=0$ by [F3].
Hence
$\|c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\|^2
=\langle\Omega_D,c(u)c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\rangle_2
=\langle\Omega_D,(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))\Omega_D\rangle_2=1$.
A second creation vanishes. Since vacuum and one-particle sectors are
orthogonal, the cyclic subspace generated by $u$ is exactly
$\operatorname{span}\{\Omega_D,c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\}$. Moreover,
$N_u^*=N_u$ and
$N_u^2=c^\dagger(u)(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))c(u)=N_u$ because
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. Thus $N_u$ is a projection, so its only possible
eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$; it acts as $0$ on $\Omega_D$ and as $1$ on
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$. [A1, A2, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Since $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ are mutual adjoints on the finite-sector
vectors, $\|v_{n+1}\|^2=\langle v_n,a(h)a^\dagger(h)v_n\rangle_2
=(n+1)\|v_n\|^2$. Starting from $\|v_0\|=1$ gives $\|v_n\|^2=n!$.
The vectors $v_n$ lie in distinct Fock sectors and are orthogonal.
Consequently the displayed $|n\rangle_h$ are orthonormal, and dividing
$a(h)v_n=n v_{n-1}$ by the factorial normalizations gives
$a(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle_h$. The creation formula gives
$a^\dagger(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt{n+1}|n+1\rangle_h$, and applying $a^\dagger$
to the annihilation formula gives $N_h|n\rangle_h=n|n\rangle_h$.
[A2, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The scalar ladder and Dirac one-mode exclusion above follow only after
the species-to-Fock assignments in [A1] are made. The argument uses the
specified representations and proves no relation assigning statistics to
every relativistic field. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2, given] ∎

## Example

Choose a unit scalar wave-packet mode $h$ and a unit Dirac particle or
antiparticle mode $u$. The states and operators below are those of the
conditional model theorem [[pthm-qft-free-fock-statistics]].

For the bosonic mode, let $|n\rangle_h$ be the normalized $n$-occupation
vector. We also construct a normalized Fock vector whose annihilation image
is not square-summable, so the maximal annihilation operator is not defined
on every Fock vector.

For the fermionic mode, the one-particle vector
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$ has unit norm, while two creations in that same mode
vanish. This calculation concerns one normalized CAR mode in the adopted
representation; it is not a general spin-statistics argument.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice [A1], the scalar mode conclusion [F1], the CAR
and exact annihilation domain [F2], and the Fock-sector definitions [F3].
The modes $h$ and $u$ are supplied unit vectors.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[pthm-qft-free-fock-statistics]] proves that for each unit scalar mode
$h$, $|n\rangle_h=(a^\dagger(h))^n\Omega_s/\sqrt{n!}$ is normalized and
satisfies the bosonic ladder.

[F2] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] gives the CAR
$c(u)c^\dagger(u)+c^\dagger(u)c(u)=I$ and
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$ for a unit mode, and states that both operators are
bounded on the whole Fock space.

[F3] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] defines the vacuum as
$\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$, states $c(u)\Omega=0$, and gives the sector
insertion and contraction formulas. The finite-particle domain is dense.

[F4] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] states the exact maximal annihilation domain
$D(a(h))=\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$.

## Verification

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F4], and the chosen normalized modes $h$ and $u$.

1.1 Let $S_2=\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^{-2}$. For each $j\ge0$, the block
$2^j\le k<2^{j+1}$ contains $2^j$ terms, each at most $2^{-2j}$, so its
sum is at most $2^{-j}$. Summing these geometric bounds proves
$1\le S_2<\infty$. Therefore $C=S_2^{-1/2}$ is a positive finite constant,
and the orthonormal bosonic mode states from [F1] give
$\Psi=\sum_{n=0}^\infty C(n+1)^{-1}|n\rangle_h$ with
$\|\Psi\|^2=C^2S_2=1$. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 For $\xi_n$ in the $n$th antisymmetric sector and $\eta_{n+1}$ in the
next sector, the insertion formula, $P_{a,n+1}\eta_{n+1}=\eta_{n+1}$, and
self-adjointness of this orthogonal projection give
$\langle c^\dagger_n(u)\xi_n,\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2
=\sqrt{n+1}\langle u\otimes\xi_n,\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2
=\langle\xi_n,\sqrt{n+1}(C_u\otimes I^{\otimes n})\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2
=\langle\xi_n,c_{n+1}(u)\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2$ by the tensor product pairing
and contraction formula in [F3]. Summing over finite-sector vectors proves
$\langle c^\dagger(u)\xi,\eta\rangle_2=
\langle\xi,c(u)\eta\rangle_2$ there. Boundedness in [F2] and density in [F3]
extend this identity to the full Fock space, so
$c^\dagger(u)=c(u)^*$. The CAR, vacuum relation, and nilpotence in [F2]–[F3]
then give
$\|c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\|^2
=\langle\Omega_D,c(u)c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\rangle_2
=\langle\Omega_D,(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))\Omega_D\rangle_2=1$.
Thus the one-mode state is normalized and a second creation in that mode is
zero. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By the ladder in [F1], the squared norm of the annihilation-sector
sequence for this vector is
$C^2\sum_{n=1}^\infty n/(n+1)^2$. Since $n+1\le2n$ for $n\ge1$,
$n/(n+1)^2\ge1/(4n)$. Each dyadic block
$2^j\le n<2^{j+1}$ contributes at least $1/2$ to the harmonic series, so
$\sum_{n\ge1}1/n$ diverges and therefore
$\sum_{n\ge1}n/(n+1)^2=\infty$. By [F1], the annihilation images of the
different particle sectors lie in orthogonal sectors, so this is exactly
$\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2$. The exact domain in [F4] now gives
$\Psi\notin D(a(h))$, despite $\Psi$ being a normalized Fock vector.
[A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The adjoint identity and CAR in [F2] give $N_u^*=N_u$ and
$N_u^2=c^\dagger(u)(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))c(u)=N_u$, so $N_u$ is a projection.
The vacuum relation gives $N_u\Omega_D=0$, while
$N_uc^\dagger(u)\Omega_D=c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$. Thus its eigenvalues on
the one-mode subspace are $0$ and $1$. These are conditional model-state
calculations, not measured outcomes. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the data of [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]], and the $L^2$ and density results below.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; only countably many representatives are selected in the completion argument.

[F1] [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $H_N$ is complex $L^2$ with first-variable-linear integral pairing, $D_0=C_c^\infty$, and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$.

[F2] [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]: under Countable Choice, $H_N$ is complete for $\|\cdot\|_2$ and $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u\overline v\,dq$ is its inner product.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ in $H_N$.

[F4] [[thm-c-c-infinity-rn-is-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]]: under Countable Choice and for $p=2$, $D_0$ is dense in $H_N$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $W+1\ge2$ and every $a_j>0$, $a$ is a Hermitian positive-definite sesquilinear form on $D_0$: in particular $a(u,u)=\sum_j a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2\ge2\|u\|_2^2$, and $a(u,u)=0$ forces $u=0$ in $H_N$. Thus its Cauchy-sequence completion with the stated equivalence relation is a well-defined inner-product space. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 To see that the completion is complete, let $(X_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence of its classes. By [A1], choose $u_n\in D_0$ with $\|[u_n]-X_n\|_Q<2^{-n}$ for each $n$. The triangle inequality makes $(u_n)$ $Q$-Cauchy; its class $X$ is defined by the Cauchy-sequence construction, and $\|X_n-X\|_Q\le2^{-n}+\|[u_n]-X\|_Q\to0$. Hence $Q$ is complete and therefore Hilbert. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a $Q$-Cauchy representative sequence $(u_n)$, the inequalities $\|u_n-u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, $\sqrt{a_j}\|\partial_j u_n-\partial_j u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, and $\|\sqrt{W+1}(u_n-u_m)\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$ show that $u_n$, each $\partial_j u_n$, and $\sqrt{W+1}u_n$ converge in $L^2$ by [F2]; write their limits as $u$, $g_j$, and $h$. The first limit defines a continuous map $Q\to H_N$, since $\|u\|_2\le\|[u_n]\|_Q$, and equivalent Cauchy sequences have the same $L^2$ limit. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For every $\varphi\in D_0$, integration by parts gives $\int u_n\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int (\partial_j u_n)\overline\varphi$. Passing to the limit in both integrals by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\int u\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$, so $g_j$ is the stated weak derivative. [step 2.2, F2, F3, algebra]

3.2 On each compact ball $B_R$, the continuous polynomial $W+1$ is bounded. Therefore $\sqrt{W+1}u_n\to\sqrt{W+1}u$ in $L^2(B_R)$, while the same sequence converges there to $h$; uniqueness of limits gives $h=\sqrt{W+1}u$ almost everywhere on every integer-radius ball and hence almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^N$. Taking limits of the component norms in $a(u_n,u_n)$ now gives the displayed formula for $\|u\|_Q^2$. [step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 If $u=0$ in $L^2$, then step 3.1 says $\langle g_j,\varphi\rangle=0$ for every $\varphi\in D_0$; this pairing is continuous by [F3] and $D_0$ is dense by [F4], so it vanishes on all of $H_N$, and taking $\varphi=g_j$ gives $g_j=0$. Step 3.2 then gives $h=0$; the norm formula yields $\|[u_n]\|_Q=0$, so the embedding is injective. Finally its image contains $D_0$, which is dense in $H_N$ by [F4]; thus the continuous injection has dense image and all claims follow. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $N\ge1$, $a_j,c>0$, Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb R^N$, and the specified form completion $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; the imported basis and Hilbert expansions are used under this hypothesis.

[F1] [[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]: the completion for $a_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is a Hilbert space, injects continuously into $L^2$, and its completed norm records the weak derivatives and weighted function.

[F2] [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]]: for $\hbar,m_j,\omega_j>0$, the product Hermite functions form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb R^N)$, and on each product function the differential expression $-\hbar^2\partial_j^2/(2m_j)+m_j\omega_j^2q_j^2/2$ has eigenvalue $\hbar\omega_j(n_j+1/2)$; [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]: $g_0(y)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^2/2}$; [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]: the scaling map is $Df(x)=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell)$ with $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}$.

[F3] [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]: a complete orthonormal family in a Hilbert space has norm-convergent expansion and Parseval's identity; this applies to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ once completeness there is proved.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v)|\le\|u\|_{Q_{\mathrm{osc}}}\|v\|_{Q_{\mathrm{osc}}}$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** the oscillator form, its completion, and positive coefficients $a_j,c$.

1.1 In [F2] choose $\hbar=1$, $m_j=(2a_j)^{-1}$ and $\omega_j=2\sqrt{a_jc}$. Then $\hbar^2/(2m_j)=a_j$ and $m_j\omega_j^2/2=c$. The eigenvalue from [F2] in coordinate $j$ is $\omega_j(n_j+1/2)=(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}$. Summing over the $N$ coordinates gives the displayed differential eigenvalue $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$. In the same scaling, $b_j=m_j\omega_j=\sqrt{c/a_j}$ and the normalized $n_j=0$ Gaussian becomes $(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}$; taking the product gives the stated ground representative. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Each product Hermite function is a polynomial times a Gaussian, so it and all first derivatives have finite squared integrals after multiplication by any fixed polynomial. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $|q|\le1$, $\chi=0$ on $|q|\ge2$, and $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. Such a $\chi$ can be formed from $\eta(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $\eta(s)=0$ for $s\le0$, by taking $\chi(q)=\eta(4-|q|^2)/(\eta(4-|q|^2)+\eta(|q|^2-1))$. Then $0\le\chi_R\le1$ and $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}\in C_c^\infty$. The weighted-function error is supported on $|q|>R$ and bounded in squared integral by the integrable tail $(c|q|^2+2)|\psi_{\mathbf n}|^2$, so its $L^2$ norm tends to zero. For each derivative,
$$\partial_j((1-\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n})=(1-\chi_R)\partial_j\psi_{\mathbf n}-(\partial_j\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n};$$
the first term tends to zero by its Gaussian tail and the second has norm at most $C\|\psi_{\mathbf n}\|_2/R$. Thus $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}$ converges in the form norm, proving $\psi_{\mathbf n}\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For $v\in C_c^\infty$, integration by parts and the eigenvalue identity in step 1.1 give
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(\psi_{\mathbf n},v)=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2) \langle\psi_{\mathbf n},v\rangle.$$
The left side is continuous in the form norm of $v$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and the right side is continuous since $\|v\|_2\le\|v\|_{Q_{\mathrm{osc}}}$. Density of $C_c^\infty$ in its defining completion extends the identity to every $v\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Taking $v=\psi_{\mathbf m}$ proves that $\xi_{\mathbf n}:=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2)^{-1/2}\psi_{\mathbf n}$ is orthonormal in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. If $u\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is orthogonal in this form inner product to every $\xi_{\mathbf n}$, conjugating the displayed identity gives $\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle=0$ for every $\mathbf n$. Completeness in $L^2$ from [F2] makes the image of $u$ zero, and the injective inclusion in [F1] makes $u=0$ in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Thus $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ is complete there. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Parseval in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ with the complete orthonormal family $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ gives
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,u)=\sum_{\mathbf n}(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2) |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
Parseval in $L^2$ gives $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{\mathbf n}|\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $2\|u\|_2^2$ from the first identity yields the asserted expansion of the unshifted oscillator form. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the finite-dimensional coercive form data and Hilbert space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]. The inclusion
$J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact: the closure in $H_N$ of the image of
every bounded subset of $Q$ is compact in the metric topology. The proof below
uses an explicit cube-mean approximation for each finite $N$ and does not
assume a general Rellich theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge1$, the form domain $Q$, its norm, and the injection
$J:Q\to H_N$.

[F1] [[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]: $Q$ is complete and injects densely into the complete Hilbert space $H_N$; for $u\in Q$, its weak derivatives and weighted function are in $L^2$ and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2,$$
with $W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$.

[F2] [[def-compact-linear-operator]]: a linear map is compact when the closure of the image of every bounded set is compact; it suffices to check the closed unit ball.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: on each $L^2$ space, $|\int f\overline g|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$.

[F4] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: integrable functions on sigma-finite products have equal iterated integrals; the continuous cube integrands used below are integrable.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice as inherited through [F1], the finite data, and an arbitrary $Q$-bounded set.

1.1 Let $C$ be a cube of side $\delta>0$ and $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, with $u_C:=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu$. Expanding the square and using Fubini on the finite cube gives
$$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2\,dx\,dy.$$
Telescope $u(x)-u(y)$ through the $N$ coordinate changes and use $|\sum_{j=1}^Nz_j|^2\le N\sum_j|z_j|^2$. For the $j$th change, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|D_j(x,y)|^2\le\delta\int_{\min(x_j,y_j)}^{\max(x_j,y_j)}|\partial_ju|^2$. For fixed values of the other coordinates and fixed $s\in[0,\delta]$, the measure of pairs $(x_j,y_j)$ whose segment contains $s$ is $2s(\delta-s)\le\delta^2/2$; integrating the displayed bound over the cube variables and dividing by $2|C|$ therefore yields the safe estimate
$$\|u-u_C\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le N\delta^2\sum_{j=1}^N\|\partial_j u\|_{L^2(C)}^2.$$
It applies to complex $u$ because the squared-modulus Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 For $R>0$ and $u\in Q$, the coercive weight gives
$$\int_{|q|>R}|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\int_{|q|>R}c|q|^2|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\|u\|_Q^2.$$
Thus the $L^2$ tails of the $Q$ unit ball are uniformly small for large $R$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The estimate of step 1.1 passes to every $u\in Q$: approximate $u$ in the $Q$ norm by elements of $C_c^\infty$ (the defining completion), restrict to $C$, and use [F1] to pass the $L^2$ and derivative limits. [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so the squared tail in step 1.2 is below $\varepsilon^2/16$. For the $Q$ unit ball, [F1] gives $\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2\le\sum_j a_j^{-1}$. Choose an integer $M$ large enough that $\delta:=2R/M$ satisfies $N\delta^2\sum_j a_j^{-1}<\varepsilon^2/16$, and partition $[-R,R]^N$ into the resulting finitely many cubes of side $\delta$. Summing the squared estimates of step 2.1 over these disjoint cubes bounds the total mean-approximation error by $N\delta^2\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2<\varepsilon^2/16$. The squared error outside $[-R,R]^N$ is the tail from step 1.2; thus replacing $u$ on each cube by its mean and setting it to zero outside the large cube has total squared $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon^2/8$, hence norm error below $\varepsilon/2$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, F1, choose, algebra]

4.1 For the finite partition in step 3.1, the piecewise-constant mean function $m_u$ satisfies $\|m_u\|_2^2=\sum_C|C||u_C|^2\le\sum_C\|u\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le\|u\|_2^2\le1$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F3]. Thus each mean coordinate has modulus at most $|C|^{-1/2}$, so the vectors of means lie in a bounded box in a finite-dimensional complex coordinate space. Subdivide its real-and-imaginary coordinates into finitely many boxes of sufficiently small side length so that the associated piecewise-constant functions approximate every mean vector to $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 3.1 gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball. Scaling shows that the image of every bounded $Q$ set is totally bounded. [step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra]

5.1 Let $K$ be the $H_N$ closure of the image of the $Q$ unit ball. It is complete because it is closed in the complete space $H_N$ [F1]. Suppose an open cover of $K$ has no finite subcover. For each $n\ge1$, step 4.1 supplies a finite $2^{-n-2}$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball with centers in $H_N$; the corresponding closed balls of radius $2^{-n-1}$ cover its closure $K$. Starting with $C_0=K$, choose the least ball index for which $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$ has no finite subcover. Such an index exists, since otherwise finitely many finite subcovers would cover $C_{n-1}$. Each $C_n$ is nonempty, closed, nested, and has diameter at most $2^{-n}$. For $m>n$, any point of nonempty $C_m$ lies in both selected balls, so $\|p_m-p_n\|_2\le2^{-m-1}+2^{-n-1}$; hence $(p_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $p\in H_N$. Since $C_n$ is nonempty and is contained in both $K$ and $\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$, the distance from $p_n$ to $K$ is at most $2^{-n-1}$. Therefore $\operatorname{dist}(p,K)\le\|p-p_n\|_2+2^{-n-1}\to0$; closedness of $K$ gives $p\in K$. For fixed $n$ and every $m>n$, nonempty $C_m\subseteq C_n$ has a point $y\in C_m$ with $\|p_m-y\|_2\le2^{-m-1}$. Thus there are points of $C_n$ arbitrarily close to $p$, and closedness gives $p\in C_n$. An open set of the cover containing $p$ contains $K\cap B(p,r)$ for some $r>0$; for large $n$, $\operatorname{diam}(C_n)<r$, so that one open set covers $C_n$, a contradiction. Thus $K$ is compact. All recursive ball choices are least admissible indices in finite lists. [step 4.1, F1, algebra]

6.1 Step 5.1 proves that the closed-unit-ball image under $J$ has compact closure; applying the equivalent criterion in [F2] to the linear inclusion proves that $J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact. [step 5.1, F2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and use $Q$, $H_N$, $a$, and $W$ from
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]. For each $f\in H_N$, let $Rf$ be
the unique vector of $Q$ satisfying
$$a(v,Rf)=\langle v,f\rangle_{H_N}\qquad(v\in Q),$$
and view $R$ as an operator $H_N\to H_N$ by the inclusion of
[[lem-qft-cube-poincare-compact-form-inclusion]]. Then $R$ is bounded, compact,
self-adjoint, positive, injective, and has dense range; moreover
$\|R\|\le\tfrac12$. This is the variational inverse of the shifted polynomial
form. It establishes compactness and dense range but does not itself assert a
differential-operator realization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the coercive form Hilbert space $Q$, the complex
Hilbert space $H_N$, and the compact inclusion $J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]: $a$ is a Hilbert inner product on $Q$, $\|v\|_2\le\|v\|_Q$, and $a(v,v)\ge2\|v\|_2^2$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-cube-poincare-compact-form-inclusion]]: $J:Q\to H_N$ is a compact linear inclusion.

[F3] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: under Countable Choice, every bounded linear functional on a real or complex Hilbert space is uniquely represented by pairing in the first variable; the representing vector has the same norm as the functional.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\|v\|$ in $H_N$ and in $Q$.

[F5] [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]: a bounded linear operator is a linear map $T$ with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C$.

[F6] [[def-compact-linear-operator]]: a linear operator is compact when every bounded set has image with compact closure.

[F7] [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]: for a bounded operator on a Hilbert space, self-adjoint means $T^*=T$ and positive means $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x$.

[F8] [[thm-double-orthogonal-complement-is-closure]]: for a linear subspace $M$ of a Hilbert space, $M^{\perp\perp}=\overline M$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For fixed $f\in H_N$, the functional $v\mapsto\langle v,f\rangle_{H_N}$ is linear and satisfies $|\langle v,f\rangle|\le\|v\|_2\|f\|_2\le\|v\|_Q\|f\|_2$ by [F1] and Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F3] applied to the Hilbert space $(Q,a)$ gives a unique $Rf\in Q$ with the stated variational identity. For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$, conjugate-linearity in the second argument gives $a(v,\alpha Rf+\beta Rg)=\langle v,\alpha f+\beta g\rangle$, so uniqueness makes $R$ linear. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Taking $v=Rf$ in the identity gives $\|Rf\|_Q^2=a(Rf,Rf)=\langle Rf,f\rangle$. Hence $\|Rf\|_Q^2\le\|Rf\|_2\|f\|_2\le\|Rf\|_Q\|f\|_2$, so $\|Rf\|_Q\le\|f\|_2$ (with the zero case immediate). Consequently $R:H_N\to H_N$ is bounded by [F5]. [step 1.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

2.2 The same identity and $a(Rf,Rf)\ge2\|Rf\|_2^2$ give $2\|Rf\|_2^2\le\|Rf\|_2\|f\|_2$; division when $Rf\ne0$ yields $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$. If $Rf=0$, the variational identity says $\langle v,f\rangle=0$ for every $v\in Q$; since $Q$ is dense in $H_N$ by [F1], continuity of the inner product gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$. Thus $R$ is injective. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

2.3 For $f,g\in H_N$, the variational identity and conjugate symmetry of $a$ yield $\langle Rf,g\rangle=a(Rf,Rg)=\langle f,Rg\rangle$, so $R$ is self-adjoint by [F7]. Also $\langle Rf,f\rangle=a(Rf,Rf)\ge0$, so it is positive. [step 1.1, F1, F7, algebra]

3.1 The map $f\mapsto Rf$ is bounded from $H_N$ into $Q$ by step 2.1, and the inclusion $J:Q\to H_N$ is compact by [F2]. Therefore for every bounded $B\subseteq H_N$, $R(B)=J(R(B))$ has compact closure, which is exactly compactness by [F6]. [step 2.1, F2, F6]

4.1 If $z\perp\operatorname{ran}R$, then $\langle Rf,z\rangle=0$ for every $f\in H_N$. Self-adjointness from step 2.3 gives $\langle f,Rz\rangle=0$ for every $f$, so $Rz=0$ and step 2.2 gives $z=0$. Thus $(\operatorname{ran}R)^\perp=\{0\}$, and [F8] gives $\overline{\operatorname{ran}R}=(\operatorname{ran}R)^{\perp\perp}=\{0\}^\perp=H_N$. Therefore $R$ has dense range. [step 2.2, step 2.3, F8] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $H_N$, the compact positive injective operator $R$,
and its variational form.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is used to select orthonormal bases in countably many finite-dimensional eigenspaces.

[F1] [[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]: $R$ is bounded, compact, self-adjoint, positive, injective, and $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$; for each $f\in H_N$, $Rf\in Q$ is the unique vector satisfying $a(v,Rf)=\langle v,f\rangle$ for all $v\in Q$.

[F2] [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]: the nonzero eigenspaces of a compact self-adjoint operator are finite-dimensional, their eigenvalues are real with only possible accumulation point $0$, and their closed span is $(\ker R)^\perp$.

[F3] [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]: each finite-dimensional eigenspace has an orthonormal basis.

[F4] [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]: a complete orthonormal family in a Hilbert space gives norm-convergent finite-subset expansions and Parseval's identity.

[F5] [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]], [[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], and [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]: an unbounded operator has a specified linear domain; its adjoint domain consists of vectors for which the defining pairing is represented by a Hilbert-space vector; a densely defined operator is self-adjoint exactly when its domain equals its adjoint domain and the actions agree.

[F6] [[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] and [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]: $(Q,a)$ is a Hilbert space, $Q$ injects into $H_N$, and a complete orthonormal family in either Hilbert space has Parseval expansion in its Hilbert norm.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: the Hilbert-space and form pairings satisfy Cauchy--Schwarz.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], $R$ is compact and self-adjoint. Applying [F2] and using $\ker R=\{0\}$ shows that the closed span of its nonzero eigenspaces is all of $H_N$. If $R\psi=\mu\psi$ with $\psi\ne0$, then $\mu\|\psi\|^2=\langle R\psi,\psi\rangle\ge0$ by positivity, while injectivity rules out $\mu=0$; hence every nonzero eigenvalue is positive. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The domains defined by the squared coefficient sums for $E_n$ and $\lambda_n=E_n-(C_0+1)$ coincide. Indeed
$$\lambda_n^2\le2E_n^2+2(C_0+1)^2,\qquad E_n^2\le2\lambda_n^2+2(C_0+1)^2.$$
Multiplying by $|c_n|^2$ and summing preserves finiteness in both directions because $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2<\infty$ by [F4]. This proves the displayed coefficient-domain description of $D(h)$. [F4, algebra]

2.1 Each eigenspace is finite-dimensional by [F2], and so has an orthonormal basis by [F3]. The set of nonzero eigenvalues is at most countable, and [A1] selects these finite bases; their union is an orthonormal family whose closed span is $H_N$ by step 1.1. The space is infinite-dimensional: the indicators of the pairwise disjoint unit cubes $[r,r+1)\times[0,1)^{N-1}$, $r\in\mathbb N$, are nonzero mutually orthogonal $L^2$ vectors. Thus the family can be indexed by $n\ge1$. The bound $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$ gives $0<\mu_n\le\tfrac12$ and $E_n\ge1$. The compact spectral theorem says only finitely many eigenvalues satisfy $\mu\ge\varepsilon$ for each $\varepsilon>0$; recursively taking a largest remaining eigenvalue (which exists because above half its positive supremum there are only finitely many) orders them nonincreasingly with multiplicity and gives $\mu_n\to0$, hence $E_n\to\infty$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The family $(\psi_n)$ is complete by step 1.1, so [F4] gives $u=\sum_n\langle u,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n$ in norm for every $u\in H_N$ and Parseval. In particular $D(S)$ is dense because it contains all finite linear combinations of the $\psi_n$. Since each $E_n$ is real, the diagonal formula for $S$ gives $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,Sv\rangle$ for finite sums, and then for all $u,v\in D(S)$ by [F7] and convergence of the coefficient series; thus $S$ is symmetric. For $u\in D(S)$ with coefficients $c_n$, Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] makes $\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2$ absolutely convergent, and step 2.1 gives $E_n\ge1$, so $\langle Su,u\rangle=\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2\ge\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2$. [F4, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 To compute the adjoint domain, let $v=\sum_nd_n\psi_n\in D(S^*)$ and write $S^*v=z=\sum_nz_n\psi_n$. Testing the adjoint identity on each $\psi_n$ gives $z_n=E_nd_n$. Because $z\in H_N$, Parseval gives $\sum_nE_n^2|d_n|^2<\infty$, so $v\in D(S)$. Conversely, if this sum is finite, then $z:=\sum_nE_nd_n\psi_n\in H_N$ and the coefficient identity $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,z\rangle$ holds first for finite sums and then for every $u\in D(S)$ by [F7]; hence $v\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*v=Sv$. Therefore $D(S^*)=D(S)$ and $S^*=S$ as operators; by the unbounded self-adjointness definition in [F5], $S$ is self-adjoint. [F4, F5, F7, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 On each $\psi_n$, $(S+I)^{-1}\psi_n=(E_n+1)^{-1}\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n=R\psi_n$. Both sides are bounded operators on $H_N$ and agree on the span of the complete family, so they agree on all of $H_N$. Thus $(S+I)^{-1}=R$, which is compact by [F1]. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 The variational identity for $R$, applied to $f=\psi_n$, gives $a(v,R\psi_n)=\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ for every $v\in Q$. Since $R\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n$ and $\mu_n>0$, each $\psi_n$ lies in $Q$ and
$$a(v,\psi_n)=\mu_n^{-1}\langle v,\psi_n\rangle.$$
Thus $\xi_n:=\sqrt{\mu_n}\,\psi_n$ is an orthonormal family in $Q$. If $v\in Q$ is orthogonal in $a$ to every $\xi_n$, the displayed identity makes all $H_N$ coefficients $\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ zero. The $H_N$ completeness of $(\psi_n)$ and injectivity of $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ force $v=0$ in $Q$. Hence $(\xi_n)$ is complete in $Q$, and Parseval in $(Q,a)$ gives
$$a(v,v)=\sum_n\mu_n^{-1}|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2=\sum_n(E_n+1)|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
[F1, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.2, algebra]

5.2 Let $u\in C_c^\infty$ and set $f:=(-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2+W+1)u\in H_N$. Integration by parts gives $a(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for $v\in C_c^\infty$; both sides are continuous in $v$ for the $Q$ norm by [F7], and $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $Q$, so the identity holds for all $v\in Q$. It is the defining variational identity for $Rf$, and uniqueness in [F1] gives $Rf=u$. Hence $u\in\operatorname{ran}R=D(S)$ and $(S+I)u=f$, so $Su=-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2u+Wu$. [F1, F7, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Parseval in $H_N$ gives $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_n|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $(C_0+2)$ times this identity from step 5.1 yields the claimed formula for $q_h(v)$, because $E_n+1-(C_0+2)=E_n-C_0-1=\lambda_n$. [step 5.1, F4, algebra]

6.2 If $u\in D(h)=D(S)$ and $c_n=\langle u,\psi_n\rangle$, then $\sum_nE_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$ by the definition of $D(S)$. Since $E_n\ge1$, $E_n+1\le2E_n^2$, so $\sum_n(E_n+1)|c_n|^2<\infty$. Step 5.1 therefore gives $u\in Q$. Thus every eigenvector, and indeed every operator-domain vector, belongs to the form domain. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Subtracting the real scalar $(C_0+1)I$ preserves self-adjointness on the same domain, and $E_n\ge1$ gives eigenvalues $\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1\ge-C_0$. For $u\in D(h)$, the diagonal expansion and Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] make $\langle hu,u\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2$ absolutely convergent; Parseval then gives $\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$. The lowest eigenvalue corresponds to the largest eigenvalue $\mu_1$ of $R$; its eigenspace is nonzero and finite-dimensional by [F2]. Since $W=V+C_0+1$, step 5.2 shows that $h=S-(C_0+1)I$ extends the specified polynomial differential expression. Finally $h+(C_0+2)I=S+I$, whose inverse is the compact operator $R$ by step 4.2. These statements establish the declared realization and all listed scope limits. [F1, F2, F7, step 2.1, step 4.2, step 5.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and use $Q$, $q_h$, and the operator $h$ from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\lambda_1$ be the least
eigenvalue of $h$. Then
$$\inf\{q_h(u):u\in Q,\ \|u\|_2=1\}=\lambda_1.$$
The infimum is attained by every normalized vector in the lowest eigenspace;
no simplicity or nondegeneracy is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the form domain $Q$, the form $q_h$, and the complete eigenfamily of $h$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: countable eigenbasis choices used in the form realization are permitted.

[F1] [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]: the eigenvalues $\lambda_n$ are real, ordered increasingly with multiplicity, have a least value $\lambda_1$, and for $u\in Q$,
$$q_h(u)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$

[F2] [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]: $\sum_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2=\|u\|_2^2$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $u\in Q$ and the ordered real eigenvalue list.

1.1 Since $\lambda_n\ge\lambda_1$ for every $n$, [A1], [F1] and [F2] imply
$$q_h(u)-\lambda_1\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_n(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2\ge0.$$
Thus every unit vector in $Q$ has form value at least $\lambda_1$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 A normalized eigenvector $\psi_1$ belongs to $D(h)\subseteq Q$ by
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]], has norm one, and its sole
nonzero coefficient is at an eigenvalue $\lambda_1$. Therefore
$q_h(\psi_1)=\lambda_1$, so the lower bound is attained and equals the
infimum. If the lowest eigenspace has dimension greater than one, the same
coefficient calculation applies to every normalized vector in it. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and use one fixed one-mode regulator with
dimensionless $a>0$, $r>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$. Here $r$ is a polynomial
coefficient, not an SI rest mass. Take
$V_\lambda(q)=\frac{r^2}{2}q^2+\lambda q^4$ on
$H_1=L^2(\mathbb R,dq;\mathbb C)$, with the form realization from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\epsilon_g(\lambda)$
be its least eigenvalue. The physical ground-energy prediction for the
adopted scale $E_*>0$ joules is
$E_g^{\rm phys}(\lambda):=E_*\epsilon_g(\lambda)$. Then

$$0\le E_g^{\rm phys}(\lambda)-E_g^{\rm phys}(0)\le \frac{3E_*a\lambda}{2r^2}.$$

For $\lambda>0$ this is an interacting one-mode model on the full
$L^2(\mathbb R)$ space. The inequality is an exact fixed-regulator model
deduction; it supplies neither an observed energy nor a perturbation-series
or continuum-limit claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $a>0$, $r>0$, $\lambda\ge0$; the one-mode
form realizations; and $E_*>0$ joules.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a
choice function. The QFT-IR01 spectral and variational suppliers assume this
principle.

[A2] [[post-qft-regulated-polynomial-model]]: $q$ is dimensionless,
$E_*>0$ is a primitive energy scale in joules, and a self-adjoint form
realization $h$ gives $H_{\rm phys}=E_*h$.

[A3] [[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]: physical interpretation
of a Hamiltonian as the selected model's energy operator is adopted only
after that self-adjoint operator has actually been constructed.

[F1] [[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]: for a real polynomial $V$
with $V(q)\ge c q^2-C_0$, the form domain is the completion of
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ in the norm
$\|u\|_Q^2=a\|u'\|_2^2+\int(V+C_0+2)|u|^2dq$, and it injects into $L^2$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]]: for $N=1$, coefficients
$a>0,c>0$, the oscillator form with potential $cq^2$ has normalized ground
function $g_b(q)=(b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bq^2/2}$,
$b=\sqrt{c/a}$, ground eigenvalue $\sqrt{ac}$, and the proof supplies smooth
compact cutoffs with derivative bounded by $C/R$.

[F3] [[lem-qft-regulated-ground-variational-bound]]: under Countable Choice,
the least eigenvalue of each selected coercive form realization is the
infimum of its form values on normalized vectors in its form domain.

[F4] [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]: under Countable Choice
and the coercive polynomial hypotheses, the selected form realization is
self-adjoint with compact resolvent, and its lowest eigenvalue is attained.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $V_\lambda(q)=r^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4\ge (r^2/2)q^2$, the
coercivity hypotheses of [F1] and [F4] hold with $c=r^2/2$ and $C_0=0$.
Countable Choice [A1] therefore gives the form domains of [F1] and the
self-adjoint compact-resolvent form realizations with attained least
eigenvalues from [F4], for both $q_\lambda$ and $q_0$.
[A1, F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 On $C_c^\infty$, the shifted form norms obey
$\|u\|_{Q_0}^2\le\|u\|_{Q_\lambda}^2$ because their difference is
$\lambda\int q^4|u|^2dq\ge0$. Hence the identity extends continuously
$Q_\lambda\to Q_0$, and the two continuous injections into $L^2$ identify
the same representative. On the core,
$q_\lambda(u)=q_0(u)+\lambda\int q^4|u|^2dq\ge q_0(u)$; approximating any
$u\in Q_\lambda$ by core elements and using continuity of both forms passes
this inequality to $u$. For a normalized $u$, [F3] gives
$q_0(u)\ge\epsilon_g(0)$, so taking the infimum on $Q_\lambda$ yields
$\epsilon_g(\lambda)\ge\epsilon_g(0)$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $g_b(q)=(b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bq^2/2}$ with $b=r/\sqrt{2a}$, the
normalized ground function in [F2] for $c=r^2/2$. Choose the smooth cutoff
$\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ from [F2], with $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$,

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and let $h$ be the self-adjoint operator of
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]], with complete orthonormal
eigenfamily $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$ and real eigenvalues
$\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1$. For $t\in\mathbb R$ define
$$U(t)f:=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-it\lambda_n}\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n \qquad(f\in H_N).$$
Then the series converges in $H_N$ for every $f$; $U(t)$ is unitary,
$U(0)=I$, $U(s+t)=U(s)U(t)$, and $t\mapsto U(t)f$ is norm-continuous for
every $f$. Its norm derivative at any $t$ exists exactly for $f\in D(h)$, and
then
$$\frac{d}{dt}U(t)f=-i\,hU(t)f.$$
This is a mathematical one-parameter group with a dimensionless real
parameter; it makes no physical unit or empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $H_N$; the self-adjoint $h$; its eigenvectors and real eigenvalues.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: countable selections used in the eigenbasis construction are permitted.

[F1] [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]: $(\psi_n)$ is a complete orthonormal eigenfamily of $h$, $h\psi_n=\lambda_n\psi_n$, and $D(h)=\{f:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^2<\infty\}$.

[F2] [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]: expansions in the complete orthonormal family converge in norm and Parseval identifies the squared norm with the coefficient-square sum.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: every coefficient functional $f\mapsto\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$ is continuous.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $f\in H_N$, its coefficients $c_n=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$, and the real sequence $(\lambda_n)$.

1.1 Parseval gives $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, the finite partial sums defining $U(t)f$ are Cauchy in $H_N$, so converge; Parseval gives $\|U(t)f\|^2=\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. The coefficient formula shows $U(-t)U(t)f=f=U(t)U(-t)f$ and $U(s)U(t)f=U(s+t)f$, first on finite sums and then on all of $H_N$ by norm convergence and the norm bound. Thus $U(t)$ is a surjective isometry, hence unitary, and $U(0)=I$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Fix $s\in\mathbb R$ and $f\in H_N$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F\subset\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2<\varepsilon^2/64$, possible by convergence of the nonnegative series in [F2]. The norm of the difference on the complement is at most $2(\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2)^{1/2}<\varepsilon/4$. On the finite set $F$, each scalar $e^{-it\lambda_n}$ is continuous in $t$, so the finite partial difference has norm below $3\varepsilon/4$ for $t$ sufficiently close to $s$. The triangle inequality proves $\|U(t)f-U(s)f\|<\varepsilon$, establishing strong continuity. [F2, algebra]

1.3 Let $f\in D(h)$, so $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, $U(t)f$ has the same finite weighted coefficient sum and belongs to $D(h)$. For $r\ne0$,
$$\frac{U(t+r)f-U(t)f}{r} =\sum_ne^{-it\lambda_n}\frac{e^{-ir\lambda_n}-1}{r}c_n\psi_n.$$
The scalar integral identity $e^{-ir\lambda}-1=\int_0^r(-i\lambda)e^{-is\lambda}\,ds$ gives $|(e^{-ir\lambda}-1)/r|\le|\lambda|$. Thus the difference quotient coefficients are dominated in square sum by $\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2$. On each finite set they converge to $-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n$; choosing a finite set with small tail in that dominating series and then taking $r\to0$ proves convergence in $H_N$ to $-i\sum_n\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n\psi_n=-ihU(t)f$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, suppose the norm derivative at $t=0$ exists and equals $g\in H_N$. Continuity of the coefficient functional $v\mapsto\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ from [F3] makes its value on the difference quotient converge to $-i\lambda_nc_n$. Hence $\langle g,\psi_n\rangle=-i\lambda_nc_n$ for every $n$. Parseval for $g$ implies $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2=\|g\|^2<\infty$, so $f\in D(h)$ by [F1]. If the derivative exists at any other $t$, the same coefficient argument multiplies each coefficient by a unit phase and yields the identical summability condition. Thus the differentiability domain is exactly $D(h)$ at every $t$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

1.3 Since $\Gamma(p+k)-\Gamma(p)=\Gamma(k)$, the resolvent identity [F3] with $A=K(p)$, $B=K(p+k)$ gives $S_0(p+k)\Gamma(k)S_0(p)=S_0(p)-S_0(p+k)$. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

1.4 For off-shell $p_0,\ldots,p_N$, put $k_j=p_{j+1}-p_j$. Applying [step 1.3] at each adjacent pair yields $S_0(p_{j+1})\Gamma(k_j)S_0(p_j)=S_0(p_j)-S_0(p_{j+1})$; summing $j=0,\ldots,N-1$ cancels each interior term and leaves $S_0(p_0)-S_0(p_N)$. [step 1.3, algebra]

2.1 If $K(p)u(p)=0$, then taking the adjoint and using $\beta K(p)^\dagger\beta=K(p)$ from [step 1.1] gives $\bar u(p)K(p)=0$. The same calculation applied to $(\Gamma(q)+\mu)v(q)=0$ gives $\bar v(q)(\Gamma(q)+\mu)=0$. [A2, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For $k=p-p'$, $\Gamma(k)=\Gamma(p)-\Gamma(p')$; the right equation for $u(p)$ and left equation for $\bar u(p')$ from [step 2.1] therefore give $\bar u(p')\Gamma(k)u(p)=\mu\bar u(p')u(p)-\mu\bar u(p')u(p)=0$. For $k=p+q$, $\Gamma(k)=\Gamma(p)+\Gamma(q)$; the right $u$ equation and left $v$ equation give $\bar v(q)\Gamma(k)u(p)=\mu\bar v(q)u(p)-\mu\bar v(q)u(p)=0$. [A2, F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For any $\mu>0$, use $h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, $p=(0,0,0,0)$, and $k=(2\mu,0,0,0)$. Both $p$ and $p+k$ are off shell. The exact rational matrices are
$$ S_0(p)=-\frac{1}{\mu}I_4,\qquad S_0(p+k)=\frac{2\beta+I_4}{3\mu},\qquad \Gamma(k)=2\mu\beta . $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mu>0$, $p=0$, $k=(2\mu,0,0,0)$, and the Dirac matrices in [[lem-qft-qed-tree-ward]].

[F1] [[lem-qft-qed-tree-ward]]: when both $h(p,p)-\mu^2$ and $h(p+k,p+k)-\mu^2$ are nonzero, $S_0(p)=(\Gamma(p)+\mu I_4)/(h(p,p)-\mu^2)$ and $S_0(p+k)\Gamma(k)S_0(p)=S_0(p)-S_0(p+k)$.

[F2] [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]: $\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)$, so $\beta^2=I_4$; the item fixes $\Gamma(p)$ with the effective matrix $h=-\eta$.

[A1] $\mu>0$ has inverse-length units; the momenta $p=0$ and $k=(2\mu,0,0,0)$ use the same inverse-length coordinate convention as [[lem-qft-qed-tree-ward]].

## Verification

**Given:** [F1], [F2], and the numerical momenta and positive parameter in the Example.

1.1 Here $h(p,p)-\mu^2=-\mu^2$ and $h(p+k,p+k)-\mu^2=3\mu^2$, so both rational inverses are defined. Since $\Gamma(p)=0$ and $\Gamma(k)=2\mu\beta$, the inverse formula in [F1] gives the displayed $S_0(p)$ and $S_0(p+k)$. [A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 Using $\beta^2=I_4$ from [F2],
$$ S_0(p+k)\Gamma(k)S_0(p) =-\frac{(2\beta+I_4)2\beta}{3\mu} =-\frac{4I_4+2\beta}{3\mu} =S_0(p)-S_0(p+k). $$
Thus this off-shell rational instance satisfies the exact matrix Ward identity. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $n\in S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$, let $E_n=n^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(I-nn^T)$ be the real transverse plane. There do not exist continuous maps $e_1,e_2:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ such that, for every $n$, $(e_1(n),e_2(n))$ is an orthonormal basis of $E_n$. A continuous real orthonormal polarization frame would in particular give a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the transverse fiber is $E_n=n^\perp$; and the published even-sphere tangent-field theorem.

[A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The real range of $P_T(n)=I-nn^T$ is exactly $n^\perp$. [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]

[F2] For every positive even $d$, there is no continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^d$. [[thm-no-nowhere-zero-tangent-vector-field-on-an-even-sphere]]

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 If such a frame existed, then $e_1(n)\in n^\perp$ for every $n$ by [F1], and $|e_1(n)|=1$ by orthonormality. Therefore $e_1$ is a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Since $2$ is a positive even integer, [F2] forbids the vector field produced in step 1.1. This contradiction proves the nonexistence of the global frame. [A1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For each nonzero $\mathbf k$, the physical photon fiber is the real plane $n^\perp$ (or its complexification), where $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$, and therefore has dimension two. Locally in direction space one can choose two continuous orthonormal polarization vectors. There is no continuous real orthonormal polarization frame on all of $S^2$. In the Lorenz auxiliary construction, the four-component subsidiary space modulo its null radical is isometric to this same two-dimensional transverse fiber; four auxiliary components do not represent four positive physical polarizations.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the transverse projection, the subsidiary quotient, and the no-global-frame lemma.

[A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The range of $P_T(n)=I-nn^T$ is the rank-two plane $n^\perp$. [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]

[F2] The subsidiary quotient $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ is isometric to the positive transverse space, and the auxiliary fiber has null line $\mathbb C(1,n)$. [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]

[F3] The transverse planes over $S^2$ admit no global continuous real orthonormal frame. [[lem-qft-photon-no-global-polarization-frame]]

[F4] The cross product is orthogonal to both factors and satisfies $\|u\times v\|^2=\|u\|^2\|v\|^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2$. [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] [[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]]

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Since $n$ is unit, $P_T(n)=I-nn^T$ has kernel $\mathbb R n$ and range $n^\perp$, of dimension $3-1=2$, by [F1]. For any fixed unit vector $u$ not parallel to $n_0$, $P_T(n)u$ is nonzero on a neighborhood of $n_0$; there define $e_1(n)=P_T(n)u/|P_T(n)u|$ and $e_2(n)=n\times e_1(n)$. By [F4], $e_2$ is orthogonal to both unit vectors and $|e_2|^2=1-0=1$. It is therefore a continuous unit vector in $n^\perp$, orthogonal to $e_1$, so the two vectors form a local frame. [A1, F1, F4, given, construct]

1.2 The quotient in [F2] is positive and isometric to the range in step 1.1, so it has exactly two physical directions in each nonzero momentum fiber. A global continuous real frame would contradict [F3]. Thus the local construction cannot be made into a single continuous frame over the whole sphere. [F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the model data of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]]. The nonnegative electric operator $H_0=\lambda_E\sum_e E_e^2$ is self-adjoint on the stated maximal diagonal domain and finite Fourier/occupation sums are a graph core. The finite plaquette and fermion interaction $V=V_B+V_F$ is bounded and self-adjoint. Therefore $H=H_0+V$ is self-adjoint on exactly $D(H_0)$. Moreover $H$ commutes with every gauge transformation $U(\alpha)$ on this domain. No continuum-limit assertion follows.



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite graph, joint Fourier/occupation basis, coefficients, operators, and domain in [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]].

[F1] [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]]: $H_0$ is multiplication by $\lambda_E\sum_e n_e^2$ on the maximal diagonal domain; $W_p$ is a finite product of link multiplication unitaries; $V_B,V_F$ are finite sums of the displayed plaquette and CAR terms. The model definition records the exact conditional statement and current draft status of its CAR supplier.

## Proof

**Given:** The data and operator domains in [F1], with $\lambda_E>0$.

1.1 In the joint basis, $H_0$ multiplies coefficients by the real nonnegative number $h(\mathbf n)=\lambda_E\sum_e n_e^2$. If $\phi\in D(H_0^*)$ with $H_0^*\phi=\eta$, testing against each basis vector gives $\eta_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}=h(\mathbf n)\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}$, so $\eta\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ forces $\sum h(\mathbf n)^2|\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty$ and $\phi\in D(H_0)$. Conversely that weighted square summability and Cauchy–Schwarz give the adjoint identity. Hence $H_0^*=H_0$. Truncating a vector to finite subsets of the joint basis converges both in norm and in the $H_0$ graph norm, so finite sums are a graph core. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Every $W_p$ is unitary, so $\|W_p+W_p^\dagger\|\le2$ and $W_p+W_p^\dagger$ is self-adjoint. Each CAR operator has norm at most one by the conditional supplier in [F1]; every displayed fermion/link term is a finite sum of products of bounded operators, and pairing each term with its adjoint makes $V_F$ self-adjoint. Since the graph, plaquette list, site modes, and matrices are all finite-dimensional or finite in number, $V$ is bounded and self-adjoint. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\beta>\|V\|$ and $z=\pm i\beta$. The diagonal resolvent $R_0(z)=(H_0-z)^{-1}$ satisfies $\|R_0(z)\|\le1/\beta$, and $$H-z=(I+VR_0(z))(H_0-z).$$ The Neumann series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-VR_0(z))^k$ converges in operator norm because $\|VR_0(z)\|<1$, so $I+VR_0(z)$ is onto and invertible. Thus both $H-i\beta$ and $H+i\beta$ are onto $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On $D(H_0)$, $H$ is densely defined and symmetric because $H_0$ and $V$ are. To prove self-adjointness directly, take $y\in D(H^*)$ and choose $x\in D(H)$ with $(H+i\beta)x=(H^*+i\beta)y$, using the surjectivity from step 3.1. Then $y-x\in\ker(H^*+i\beta)=\operatorname{Ran}(H-i\beta)^\perp=\{0\}$, again by step 3.1. Therefore $D(H^*)\subseteq D(H)$; symmetry gives the reverse inclusion and $H=H^*$. Its domain is exactly the original $D(H_0)$ because the sum with bounded $V$ was defined there. [step 3.1, step 2.1, algebra]

5.1 Each $U(\alpha)$ is diagonal in the same Fourier/occupation basis as $H_0$, so it preserves $D(H_0)$ and commutes with $H_0$. The link relation $[E_e,U_e]=U_e$ and the CAR relation $[n_x,c_{y\beta}]=-\delta_{xy}c_{y\beta}$ give $U(\alpha)U_eU(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i(\alpha_{s(e)}-\alpha_{t(e)})}U_e$ and $U(\alpha)c_{x\beta}U(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i\alpha_x}c_{x\beta}$. A cycle's link phases telescope to $1$; in a hopping term the phases multiply to $e^{-i\alpha_{s(e)}}e^{i(\alpha_{s(e)}-\alpha_{t(e)})}e^{i\alpha_{t(e)}}=1$, and each onsite bilinear has phase $e^{-i\alpha_x}e^{i\alpha_x}=1$. Therefore $U(\alpha)VU(\alpha)^\dagger=V$ and $U(\alpha)HU(\alpha)^\dagger=H$ on $D(H_0)$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the model data of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]] and the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be the self-adjoint Hamiltonian on the exact domain supplied by [[lem-qft-lattice-hamiltonian-selfadjoint]], and let $P$ be the physical projection of [[lem-qft-lattice-gauss-projection]]. For any scalar $\hbar>0$, the family
$$\mathcal U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar},\qquad t\in\mathbb R,$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$, preserves $D(H)$, and satisfies
$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathcal U(h)\psi-\psi}{h}=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H\psi\quad(\psi\in D(H)).$$
It commutes with every gauge transformation $U(\alpha)$ and with $P$. Hence $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\operatorname{ran}P$ is a reducing subspace and $\mathcal U(t)|_{\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with skew-adjoint infinitesimal generator $-iH|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$; its self-adjoint Stone operator is $-H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$. Equivalently, the restricted physical Hamiltonian $H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}$ is self-adjoint. This is an exact fixed-graph result; no continuum dynamics are asserted.



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-graph model, its gauge representation and physical projection, the self-adjoint operator $H$, and the Axiom of Choice.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is the principle that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[lem-qft-lattice-gauss-projection]]: the operators $U(\alpha)$ form a strongly continuous unitary representation of $\mathbb T^V$ and $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto their joint fixed space $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-lattice-hamiltonian-selfadjoint]]: $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$ and $U(\alpha)HU(\alpha)^\dagger=H$ there; $U(\alpha)$ preserves that domain.

[F3] [[thm-stone-one-parameter-unitary-groups]]: assuming the Axiom of Choice, every self-adjoint operator $T$ determines the strongly continuous group $e^{itT}$, whose generator has domain exactly $D(T)$ and equals $iT$ there; a strongly continuous unitary group is uniquely determined by its generator.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and $\hbar>0$.

1.1 Since $H$ is self-adjoint, $T=-H/\hbar$ is self-adjoint. Stone's theorem [F3] gives $\mathcal U(t)=e^{itT}=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ as a strongly continuous unitary group with the stated derivative at $t=0$ and exact generator domain $D(H)$. [A1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $x\in D(H)$ and fixed $t$, the difference quotient at zero for $\mathcal U(h)\mathcal U(t)x=\mathcal U(t)\mathcal U(h)x$ equals $\mathcal U(t)(\mathcal U(h)x-x)/h$ and converges to $-i\mathcal U(t)Hx/\hbar$. The exact domain characterization in [F3] therefore gives $\mathcal U(t)x\in D(H)$ and $H\mathcal U(t)x=\mathcal U(t)Hx$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For each $\alpha$, the conjugated family $V_\alpha(t)=U(\alpha)\mathcal U(t)U(\alpha)^\dagger$ is a strongly continuous unitary group. By [F2], its generator is $-iH/\hbar$ on exactly $D(H)$, the same generator as $\mathcal U(t)$. Uniqueness in Stone's theorem gives $V_\alpha(t)=\mathcal U(t)$ for every $t$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Averaging the commutation $U(\alpha)\mathcal U(t)=\mathcal U(t)U(\alpha)$ over normalized Haar measure gives $P\mathcal U(t)=\mathcal U(t)P$. Thus $\mathcal U(t)$ and its inverse preserve $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, and the restricted group is unitary and strongly continuous on that closed Hilbert subspace. [F1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For $x\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, the restricted difference quotient is the same norm limit as in $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. It exists exactly when $x\in D(H)$ by [F3]; therefore the restricted group generator has domain $D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ and is $-iH/\hbar$ there. Stone's theorem on $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ identifies its self-adjoint Stone operator as $-H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$. Since multiplication by the nonzero real scalar $-\hbar$ preserves self-adjointness, the restricted physical Hamiltonian is self-adjoint. [A1, F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the finite-graph model of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]] and the Axiom of Choice. Let $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ be a normalized vector. A bounded operator $O$ has gauge charge $q=(q_x)_{x\in V}\in\mathbb Z^V$ when
$$U(\alpha)OU(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i\sum_x q_x\alpha_x}O.$$
Then $\langle\psi,O\psi\rangle=0$ whenever $q\ne0$, and any finite product of bounded gauge-charge eigenoperators has zero expectation when the sum of its charge vectors is nonzero.

For each $x$, if $O$ maps $D(G_x)$ into itself and $[G_x,O]$ extends to a bounded operator, then
$$\langle\psi,[G_x,O]\psi\rangle=0.$$
The same assertions apply to $O(t)=\mathcal U(t)^\dagger O\mathcal U(t)$: the finite-regulator time evolution preserves the gauge charge and the domains $D(G_x)$. These are exact operator identities for the stated regulator; no trace or path-integral identity and no continuum Ward–Takahashi statement is asserted.



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-graph gauge representation, $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, the self-adjoint gauge generators, and the Axiom of Choice.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice applies to every family of nonempty sets. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[lem-qft-lattice-gauss-projection]]: $U(\alpha)$ is strongly continuous, $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ is its fixed subspace, and the joint Fourier/occupation basis diagonalizes every $G_x$ with integer eigenvalues.

[F2] [[lem-qft-lattice-physical-evolution]]: under the Axiom of Choice, $\mathcal U(t)$ is a strongly continuous unitary group that commutes with every $U(\alpha)$ and preserves $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1], [F2], and a normalized $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$.

1.1 Physicality gives $U(\alpha)\psi=\psi$ for every $\alpha$. If $O$ has charge $q$, then $$\langle\psi,O\psi\rangle=\langle U(\alpha)\psi,O\,U(\alpha)\psi\rangle=\langle\psi,U(\alpha)^\dagger O U(\alpha)\psi\rangle=e^{-i\sum_xq_x\alpha_x}\langle\psi,O\psi\rangle.$$ If $q\ne0$, choose a vertex $x$ with $q_x\ne0$ and set $\alpha_x=\pi/q_x$, with all other components zero. The phase is $-1$, forcing $\langle\psi,O\psi\rangle=0$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}\subseteq D(G_x)$ and $O\psi\in D(G_x)$, self-adjointness of $G_x$ gives $$\langle\psi,[G_x,O]\psi\rangle=\langle G_x\psi,O\psi\rangle-\langle\psi,O G_x\psi\rangle=0.$$ If the commutator is initially defined on $D(G_x)$, its bounded extension has the same value on these vectors. [F1, given, algebra]

1.3 Fix $g\in\mathbb Z^V$ and define the joint character projection $$Q_g=\frac1{(2\pi)^{|V|}}\int_{\mathbb T^V}e^{-i\sum_xg_x\alpha_x}U(\alpha)\,d\alpha.$$ Since the joint basis diagonalizes the integer $G_x$, $Q_g$ is the orthogonal projection onto the joint eigenspace with eigenvalue vector $g$. The unitary $\mathcal U(t)$ commutes with every $U(\alpha)$ by [F2], hence with every $Q_g$. The exact domain is $$D(G_x)=\left\{\phi:\sum_{g\in\mathbb Z^V}g_x^2\|Q_g\phi\|^2<\infty\right\};$$ commutation and unitarity therefore show that $\mathcal U(t)$ preserves $D(G_x)$ and commutes there with $G_x$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 A product $O_1\cdots O_k$ of charge eigenoperators with charges $q^{(j)}$ transforms with charge $\sum_jq^{(j)}$, by inserting $U^\dagger U=I$ between adjacent factors. Applying step 1.1 to that product proves the finite-product selection rule. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Gauge covariance of $O(t)$ follows from commuting $\mathcal U(t)$ through the transformation law of $O$. Unitary conjugation preserves boundedness, and the domain relation in step 1.3 carries any $D(G_x)$ invariance and bounded commutator of $O$ to $O(t)$. The selection and infinitesimal identities already proved thus apply at every time. [F2, step 1.3, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Take a two-vertex graph with one link $e:v_1\to v_2$, one fermion mode per vertex and zero backgrounds. The zero-electric, zero-occupation vector $\Omega$ is physical. The bounded creation operator $O=c^\dagger_{v_1,1}$ has nonzero gauge charge at $v_1$, so its expectation in any physical vector, including $\Omega$, vanishes.



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The conditional finite-graph CAR model, the gauge action, and the Axiom of Choice required by the time-dependent Ward supplier.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is the principle that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[lem-qft-lattice-ward-identities]]: every bounded gauge-charge eigenoperator with nonzero charge has zero expectation in a physical vector; time evolution preserves gauge charge under AC. This current A-page item depends on the still-draft QFT-MF01 CAR supplier through its graph-model dependencies.

## Verification

**Given:** [A1], [F1], and the zero-background two-vertex state described above.

1.1 For $\Omega$, $n_{v_1}=n_{v_2}=0$ and $E_e=0$, so both Gauss eigenvalues vanish. The CAR creation operator is bounded and nonzero; the gauge law gives $U(\alpha)OU(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{-i\alpha_{v_1}}O$, so its charge vector is $q_{v_1}=-1,q_{v_2}=0$. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 The nonzero charge in step 1.1 forces $\langle\Omega,O\Omega\rangle=0$ by the finite-regulator selection rule, even though $O\Omega$ is a nonzero one-fermion vector. This demonstrates that the selection rule concerns expectations in the physical sector, not the vanishing of the charged operator itself. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume $a>0$, $m>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$, all real mathematical parameters.
For $N=1$ take the polynomial
$$V_\lambda(q)=\frac{m^2}{2}q^2+\lambda q^4$$
and the differential expression $h_\lambda=-a\,d^2/dq^2+V_\lambda(q)$ with
the form realization of [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Write
$E_g(\lambda)$ for its least eigenvalue. Then
$$0\le E_g(\lambda)-E_g(0)\le\frac{3a\lambda}{2m^2}.$$
The parameters are mathematical and dimensionless here; no physical mass,
unit, measurement, or continuum claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $a,m>0$, $\lambda\ge0$, and the finite-mode form realization for $V_\lambda$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: the spectral and form suppliers used here are invoked under Countable Choice.

[F1] [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $V_\lambda(q)\ge(m^2/2)q^2$, so $C_0=0$ and the common quadratic coercivity constant is $c=m^2/2$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]]: for $-a\,d^2/dq^2+(m^2/2)q^2$, the least eigenvalue is $m\sqrt{a/2}$ and its normalized ground function is $\phi_b(q)=(b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bq^2/2}$ with $b=m/\sqrt{2a}$.

[F3] [[lem-qft-regulated-ground-variational-bound]]: the least eigenvalue equals the infimum of the normalized form over its form domain.

[F4] [[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]: the form domain is the completion of $C_c^\infty$ for the displayed gradient-plus-weight norm and injects into $L^2$.

[F5] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: differentiation under the Gaussian integral with respect to $b>0$ is justified locally by an integrable polynomial-Gaussian bound.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $a,m>0$, $\lambda\ge0$, and the forms $q_0,q_\lambda$.

1.1 Write $a_\lambda=q_\lambda+2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ for the shifted form inner product of the $\lambda$ completion. On $C_c^\infty$, $V_\lambda\ge V_0$ gives $a_\lambda(u,u)\ge a_0(u,u)$, so a $Q_\lambda$-Cauchy sequence is $Q_0$-Cauchy and the identity extends continuously to $Q_\lambda\to Q_0$ with the same $L^2$ representative. The unshifted forms $q_\lambda=a_\lambda-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ and $q_0=a_0-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ are continuous on their respective form spaces. For any $u\in Q_\lambda$, approximate it in $Q_\lambda$ by $u_r\in C_c^\infty$; then $q_\lambda(u_r)\ge q_0(u_r)$ for every $r$, and continuity of both forms gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)$ in the limit. For normalized $u\in Q_\lambda$, [F3] then gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)\ge E_g(0)$. Taking the infimum yields $E_g(\lambda)\ge E_g(0)$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 The Gaussian $\phi_b$ from [F2] and its derivative are polynomial times a Gaussian. For cutoffs $\chi_R$ as in the cutoff construction of
[[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]], $\chi_R\phi_b\in C_c^\infty$
converges to $\phi_b$ in the $\lambda$ form norm: the derivative error is
$(1-\chi_R)\phi_b'-(\chi_R')\phi_b$, whose first term has vanishing Gaussian
tail and whose second has norm at most $C\|\phi_b\|_2/R$; the weighted error
has squared magnitude bounded by $(m^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4+2)|\phi_b|^2$, an
integrable polynomial-Gaussian tail. Thus $\phi_b\in Q_\lambda$. [A1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Let $\mathbb E_b[g]:=\int g(q)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}\,dq$. The Hermite
ground function in [F2] is normalized, so $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$. On any compact
interval of positive $b$ values, the derivatives of the integrands through
order two are bounded by a constant times $(1+|q|^4)e^{-b_*q^2}$ for some
$b_*>0$, which is integrable; [F5] therefore permits differentiation under the
integral. Differentiating $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$ gives
$$0=\mathbb E_b\!\left[\frac1{2b}-q^2\right],\qquad \mathbb E_b[q^2]=\frac1{2b}.$$

## Statement

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** [A1], the regular polynomial class, the continuous bidistribution
$W$, and the supplier statements below.

[A1] The formal parameter $\eta$ is fixed by the involution and has no
analytic or physical interpretation in this mathematical item.

[F1] A regular polynomial is a finite sum with unique symmetric test kernels;
its $k$-th derivative is the smooth compact kernel displayed in the
definition ([[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]],
[[lem-qft-tensor-test-function-density]]).

[F2] Tensor products of distributions exist as continuous distributions;
their iterated pairings associate and agree on product tests
([[thm-tensor-product-distributions-and-iterated-pairings]]).

[F3] Pairing a distribution against a smooth parameter family with locally
common compact support produces a smooth function, and derivatives pass
through the pairing ([[lem-distribution-pairing-with-smooth-parameter-families]]).

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 For each $k$, [F2] constructs $W^{\otimes k}$ on the independent variable pairs. The kernels $F^{(k)}(\phi)$ and $G^{(k)}(\phi)$ in [F1] are smooth and compactly supported, so the displayed pairing is defined. In each homogeneous term of $F$ and $G$, pairing the $k$ contracted variables leaves a smooth compact kernel in the remaining variables: the support lies in the projection of the original compact coefficient supports, and [F3] passes every remaining-variable derivative through the pairing. Thus each summand is again a regular polynomial functional. [A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 If $F$ and $G$ have degrees $m$ and $n$, then $F^{(k)}=0$ for $k>m$ and $G^{(k)}=0$ for $k>n$. Hence only $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$ contribute; the sum is finite, independent of a coefficient presentation by [F1], and belongs to $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

2.2 For $f\in\mathcal D(X)$, use the auxiliary formal generator $E_f(s,\phi)=\exp(s\ell_f(\phi))$; it is a generating series and is not asserted to be an element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$. Its $k$-th derivative in $\phi$ is $s^k f^{\otimes k}E_f$. Substitution into the finite coefficient formula gives, coefficientwise in $s,t,\eta$, $$ E_f(s)\star_W E_g(t)=\exp\!\bigl(\eta st W(f,g)\bigr)E_{sf+tg}. $$ [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Applying step 2.2 twice, both bracketings of three generators equal $$ \exp\!\bigl(\eta(stW(f,g)+srW(f,h)+trW(g,h))\bigr)E_{sf+tg+rh}, $$ by bilinearity of $W$. Comparing coefficients of $s,t,r$ proves associativity for powers of linear functionals. For distinct tests in one input, replace $f$ by $\sum_{j=1}^m s_jf_j$ in the same coefficientwise identity; its coefficient of $s_1\cdots s_m$ is the symmetrized product $\ell_{f_1}\cdots\ell_{f_m}$. Make this substitution independently in each of the three inputs. Thus the associator vanishes for every symmetrized elementary tensor-product coefficient kernel and for their finite sums. [step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By [F1], symmetrized finite product-test kernels are dense in every coefficient test space. Each fixed coefficient of the associator is a finite sum of compositions of continuous tensor-distribution pairings from [F2] and smooth parameter pairings from [F3], hence is continuous in the coefficient kernels. Passing to the limits of the product-test approximants from the preceding coefficient comparison proves associativity for arbitrary $F,G,H\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For linear functionals only $k=0,1$ occur. The $k=0$ term cancels in the commutator, while the $k=1$ terms are $\eta W(f,g)$ and $\eta W(g,f)$; this gives the displayed commutator. If $W$ is Hermitian, conjugating each finite contraction reverses its two variable groups and gives $(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $f,g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)$, let
$\ell_f(\phi)=\int f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$, and let $W$ be any continuous
bidistribution. For the regular quadratic functionals
$F(\phi)=\ell_f(\phi)^2$ and $G(\phi)=\ell_g(\phi)^2$, the finite
contraction formula is
$$ F\star_W G =\ell_f^2\ell_g^2+4\eta W(f,g)\ell_f\ell_g+2\eta^2W(f,g)^2. $$
The formula is exact in the formal parameter $\eta$.

## Example
