## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), $m_o>0$ in kilograms, $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\hbar>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Take the complete oscillator family $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ and self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H_{\rm osc}$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], with oscillator length $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_o\omega)}$ and $H_{\rm osc}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$. Let $\mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n:n\ge0\}$ be the finite Hermite span. Multiplication by position $Xf(x)=xf(x)$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself by the Hermite recurrence. Define $U(t)$ on $\mathcal C$ by $U(t)\psi_n=e^{-i\omega(n+1/2)t}\psi_n$ and extend continuously to a unitary on the oscillator Hilbert space. For $\psi_0$ the normalized ground state, define
$$C_F(t)=\frac{m_o}{\hbar}\bigl(T X(t)X(0)\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1,\qquad X(t)=U(t)^\dagger XU(t),$$
where time ordering means $T X(t)X(0)=X(t)X(0)$ for $t\ge0$ and $X(0)X(t)$ for $t<0$. Define $G_R(t)=1_{[0,\infty)}(t)\sin(\omega t)/\omega$.

Then, for every real $t$,
$$C_F(t)=\frac{e^{-i\omega|t|}}{2\omega},\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0,\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0.$$
The derivatives are distributional on $\mathbb R$, and $\delta_0(\varphi)=\varphi(0)$. Both kernels have units of seconds, so the differential identities have units of inverse seconds. In particular, $C_F(t)\ne0$ for $t<0$ while $G_R(t)=0$ there.

For a Schwartz test function $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and $\epsilon>0$, define $\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx:=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\int_{|x|>r}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ and $\delta_a(\varphi):=\varphi(a)$. The Plemelj boundary identity is
$$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x+i\epsilon}\,dx =\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}x\,dx-i\pi\varphi(0),$$
with the opposite sign of $i\epsilon$ reversing the delta sign. In this boundary formula $x$ and $\epsilon$ use one common coordinate unit. For $\nu\in\mathbb R$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the frequency regulator $\epsilon>0$ is in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $\epsilon t$ is dimensionless; the ordinary positive-sign Fourier transform of $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ its distributional limit is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left[ \operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu-\omega}-\operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu+\omega} -i\pi\delta_{\omega}-i\pi\delta_{-\omega}\right],$$
which is conventionally denoted $i/(\nu^2-\omega^2+i0)$. Here that notation means the displayed pair of opposite boundary values at the two simple poles. This one-mode result makes no spatial-causality or interacting-field claim.

Rescaling [F3] gives $$X\psi_n=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m_o\omega}}\left(\sqrt n\,\psi_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,\psi_{n+1}\right),$$ with $\psi_{-1}=0$. Thus $X$ maps the finite span $\mathcal C$ into itself, so all products in the statement are defined on $\psi_0$. On a finite vector $\sum_{n=0}^Nc_n\psi_n$, the phase rule preserves norm by orthonormality [F11]; its inverse is the opposite phase rule. Density of $\mathcal C$ follows from completeness in [F11], and Hilbert completeness [F12] gives unique continuous extensions of both inverse isometries to the whole oscillator Hilbert space. Hence $U(t)$ is unitary and agrees on $\mathcal C$ with the energy evolution [F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F10, F11, F12, algebra]

1.2 Fix $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$. Choose an even $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ equal to $1$ near zero, and put $\psi=\varphi-\varphi(0)\chi$. Then $\psi(0)=0$, and $\psi(x)/x$ is bounded near zero and integrable at infinity. The real part of the regularized integral is $$\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x\psi(x)}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\psi(x)}x\,\frac{x^2}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\,dx,$$ because the omitted $\varphi(0)\chi$ term is odd. To see convergence to $\int\psi(x)/x\,dx$, first restrict to $|x|<r$, where the difference is bounded by $2r\sup_{|x|\le r}|\psi(x)/x|$, then on $|x|\ge r$ it is bounded by $(\epsilon^2/r^2)\|\psi/x\|_1$. Let $r$ tend to zero and then $\epsilon$ tend to zero. Since $\operatorname{PV}\int\chi(x)/x\,dx=0$, this is the required principal-value real part. [given, F4, algebra]

1.3 The imaginary part is $-\int\varphi(x)\epsilon/(x^2+\epsilon^2)\,dx$. The nonnegative kernel has integral $\pi$, by the antiderivative $\arctan(x/\epsilon)$. For any $r>0$, continuity bounds the error from replacing $\varphi(x)$ by $\varphi(0)$ on $|x|\le r$ by $\pi\sup_{|x|\le r}|\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)|$. On $|x|>r$, the kernel mass is at most $2\epsilon/r$, so the error is at most $4\|\varphi\|_\infty\epsilon/r$. First choose $r$ small and then $\epsilon$ small. This proves the imaginary limit $-\pi\varphi(0)$. Replacing $+i\epsilon$ by $-i\epsilon$ reverses this sign. [given, F4, algebra]

1.4 For $\epsilon>0$, the damped kernel is integrable, and its positive-sign Fourier transform is the sum of two ordinary half-line integrals: $$\int_{\mathbb R}e^{i\nu t}e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)\,dt=\frac1{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\epsilon+i(\omega-\nu)}+\frac1{\epsilon+i(\omega+\nu)}\right)=\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$ The first equality follows by integrating $e^{-(\epsilon+i(\omega-\nu))t}$ on $t\ge0$ and $e^{-(\epsilon+i(\omega+\nu))|t|}$ on $t<0$; both real decay rates are $\epsilon>0$. [given, F5, F8, F9, algebra]

2.1 Put $d_o=\sqrt{\hbar/(2m_o\omega)}$. From step 1.1, $X\psi_0=d_o\psi_1$ and $X\psi_1=d_o(\psi_0+\sqrt2\,\psi_2)$. For $t\ge0$, applying $X(t)=U(t)^\dagger XU(t)$ to $X\psi_0$ and taking the ground-state coefficient gives $$\bigl(X(t)X\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1=d_o^2e^{-i\omega t}.$$ For $t<0$, time ordering gives $\bigl(X X(t)\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1$. Since $U(t)\psi_0=e^{-i\omega t/2}\psi_0$ and $U(t)^\dagger\psi_1=e^{3i\omega t/2}\psi_1$, step 1.1 gives $X(t)\psi_0=d_oe^{i\omega t}\psi_1$; applying $X$ and taking the ground-state coefficient gives $d_o^2e^{i\omega t}$. Multiplying by $m_o/\hbar$ and using $m_od_o^2/\hbar=1/(2\omega)$ proves $C_F(t)=e^{-i\omega|t|}/(2\omega)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, F10, algebra]

3.1 The function $C_F$ is continuous at $0$, solves $C_F''+\omega^2C_F=0$ classically on each open half-line, and has one-sided derivatives $C_F'(0+)= -i/2$ and $C_F'(0-)= i/2$. For a test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$, integrate $\int_{-\infty}^0 C_F\varphi''+\int_0^\infty C_F\varphi''$ by parts twice. The boundary terms in $\varphi'(0)$ cancel because $C_F$ is continuous; the remaining coefficient of $\varphi(0)$ is $C_F'(0+)-C_F'(0-)=-i$. Thus $(\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 The function $G_R$ is zero on $t<0$, solves $G_R''+\omega^2G_R=0$ on $t>0$, is continuous at zero with $G_R(0)=0$, and has derivative jump $G_R'(0+)-G_R'(0-)=1$. The same two integrations by parts show $(\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0$. Since $C_F(t)$ has modulus $1/(2\omega)>0$ for $t<0$ but $G_R(t)=0$ there, the Feynman kernel is not the retarded response. [given, step 2.1, F10, algebra]

4.1 To justify the distribution limit, the Fourier transform in [F6] and the rescaling in [F5] preserve the Schwartz test space. The time-side kernels $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ converge to $C_F$ against every such transformed test: on $|t|\le R$, $|e^{-\epsilon|t|}-1|\le\epsilon R$, and the tail is bounded by $(1/\omega)\int_{|t|>R}|\mathcal T_+\varphi(t)|dt$, which tends to zero as $R\to\infty$. For $\epsilon>0$, Fubini [F7] identifies the transform function in step 1.4 with this dual action, since the absolute double integral is at most $\|e^{-\epsilon|\cdot|}C_F\|_1\|\varphi\|_1$. Applying the Plemelj limits in steps 1.2 and 1.3 to the two shifted poles gives the displayed boundary distribution. Combining the rational terms at finite $\epsilon$ gives $(i+\epsilon/\omega)/(\nu^2-\omega^2+2i\epsilon\omega+\epsilon^2)$, so the numerator tends to $i$ and the two poles approach from opposite sides. In the $i0$ shorthand, the exact partial-fraction definition is $$\frac{i}{\nu^2-\omega^2+i0}:=\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i0}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i0}\right),$$ where each $i0$ is the boundary proved above; the opposite sign at the second pole follows from $\nu^2-\omega^2=(\nu-\omega)(\nu+\omega)$ and $\omega>0$. No contour integration or unproved pole rule is used. [given, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space, and let $N$, $E_N(B)$, and $P_n$ be as in
[[def-qft-x03-photon-count-pvm]]. Then $N$ is self-adjoint on its stated
domain and $E_N$ is a projection-valued measure on the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R$. It is the sector counting resolution: $E_N(B)$ keeps exactly the
sectors whose integer label lies in $B$, and $N$ multiplies sector $n$ by $n$.
For any finite Borel partition $(B_a)_{a=1}^m$ of $\mathbb R$, the projections
$E_N(B_a)$ are mutually orthogonal and sum to the identity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the square-summable symmetric Fock direct sum,
the number-operator definition, and the standard definitions of adjoint,
self-adjoint operator, and projection-valued measure.

[A1] Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] is the choice assumption of
the Fock construction used here.

[F1] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]: $\mathcal F_s(H)$ is the Hilbert direct
sum of the symmetric sectors $H_s^{(n)}$, $n\ge0$, with
$\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$; finite-sector vectors form a dense subspace.

[F2] [[def-qft-x03-photon-count-pvm]]: $D(N)=\{\Psi:\sum_n n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$,
$(N\Psi)_n=n\Psi_n$, and $(E_N(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_B(n)\Psi_n$.

[F3] [[def-projection-valued-measure]]: every value must be an orthogonal
projection, $E_N(\varnothing)=0$, $E_N(\mathbb R)=I$,
$E_N(B\cap C)=E_N(B)E_N(C)$, and disjoint countable unions must converge
strongly.

[F4] Under the second-variable-linear Fock pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], conjugating the first-variable-linear
definition in [[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]] gives:
$y\in D(N^*)$ exactly when there is $z$ such that
$\langle Nx,y\rangle_2=\langle x,z\rangle_2$ for every $x\in D(N)$; then
$N^*y=z$.

[F5] [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]:
self-adjointness means equality of the operator and its adjoint, including
equality of their domains.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F5], and the number-operator and sector-projection
formulas in [F2].

1.1 Finite-sector vectors lie in $D(N)$ and are dense by [F1]. For $\Psi,\Phi\in D(N)$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives absolute convergence of $\sum_n n\langle\Psi_n,\Phi_n\rangle_2$, and because each $n$ is real, $$\langle N\Psi,\Phi\rangle_2 =\sum_n n\langle\Psi_n,\Phi_n\rangle_2 =\langle\Psi,N\Phi\rangle_2.$$ Thus $N$ is densely defined and symmetric. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For each Borel $B$, [F2] makes $E_N(B)$ the diagonal multiplier by the real indicator $\mathbf1_B(n)$. It is bounded with norm at most one, self-adjoint, and idempotent. The same coordinate formula gives $E_N(\varnothing)=0$, $E_N(\mathbb R)=I$, and $E_N(B)E_N(C)=E_N(B\cap C)$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $y\in D(N^*)$ and write $z=N^*y$. Test [F4] on vectors supported in only sector $n$. Since $N$ acts there as $nI$, the identity for every $x_n\in H_s^{(n)}$ gives $z_n=ny_n$. Hence $\sum_n n^2\|y_n\|^2=\sum_n\|z_n\|^2<\infty$, so $y\in D(N)$ and $N^*y=Ny$. Conversely, if $y\in D(N)$, the convergent sector sum in step 1.1 gives $\langle Nx,y\rangle_2=\langle x,Ny\rangle_2$ for every $x\in D(N)$; [F4] then gives $y\in D(N^*)$ and $N^*y=Ny$. Thus $D(N^*)=D(N)$ and $N=N^*$, which proves self-adjointness by [F5]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $(B_j)_{j\ge0}$ be pairwise disjoint Borel sets with union $B$, and fix $\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H)$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $M$ so that $\sum_{n>M}\|\Psi_n\|^2<\epsilon$. Among the finitely many labels $0,\ldots,M$, each label in $B$ belongs to one $B_j$; choose $J$ at least as large as all those finitely many indices. Then $E_N(B)\Psi-\sum_{j=0}^{J}E_N(B_j)\Psi$ has zero components through sector $M$, and its squared norm is at most $\sum_{n>M}\|\Psi_n\|^2<\epsilon$. This proves strong countable additivity. Together with step 1.2 it proves the PVM clauses in [F3]. The coordinate formula in [F2] shows this PVM retains exactly the sectors on which $N$ acts by their labels. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 In a finite Borel partition $(B_a)_{a=1}^m$ of $\mathbb R$, distinct sets are disjoint, so step 1.2 gives $E_N(B_a)E_N(B_b)=0$ for $a\ne b$. Append empty sets to this finite list to apply the countable-additivity result of step 2.2; since the union is $\mathbb R$ and $E_N(\mathbb R)=I$, the finite projections sum to $I$. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

## Example

Use the one-charge prescribed current of
[[pthm-qft-example-soft-coherent-counts]] with final velocity
$v=\tfrac12$ along $\hat{\mathbf z}$. Choose any upper photon-energy cutoff
$\Lambda>0$ in joules and set $\lambda=\Lambda/\mathrm e$, where $\mathrm e$
is Euler's number. The angular coefficient is
$$C=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}(2\log 3-2)>0.$$
The exact cutoff coherent state therefore has mean photon count $C$, vacuum
probability $e^{-C}$, and mean photon energy
$C\Lambda(1-\mathrm e^{-1})$ joules. Each halving of $\lambda$ increases the
mean count by $C\log 2$; the mean energy remains bounded and tends to
$C\Lambda$ as $\lambda\downarrow0$. These are model predictions for the
prepared free state.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the coupling normalization, and the conditional

[A1] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is carried by

[F2] [[pthm-qft-example-soft-coherent-counts]]: for $0<v<1$ the prescribed

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F2], $v=\tfrac12$, $\Lambda>0$, and

## Postulate

Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat} =-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab} +\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi -(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the
SI potential rule in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. Gauge functions in the
local variation argument are compactly supported; no assertion is made about
large gauge transformations, nontrivial bundles, boundary charges, or
asymptotic sectors.

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and the positive free photon representation of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]] as the free-field correspondence used to
describe the selected species. This extra correspondence does not quantize
the interacting classical action. In particular, this postulate supplies no
interacting continuum four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, no globally
well-posed coupled PDE, no pointwise operator-valued composite current, no
scattering or LSZ construction, and no regulator-removal or
nonperturbative-existence result.

## Statement

Let $m>0$ be a particle mass in kilograms, $q\in\mathbb R$ its charge in coulombs, and $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ a smooth spatial vector potential with components in tesla-metres. Set $B_k=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iA_j$ and define on the common core $\mathcal C=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$
$$\pi_i=-i\hbar\partial_i-qA_i,\qquad H_D=c\sum_i\alpha_i\pi_i+\beta mc^2,\qquad \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i).$$
Here the matrices are those of [[lem-qft-example-spin-trace-completeness]] and $\hbar,c$ have the SI conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. These differential maps preserve $\mathcal C$, and on $\mathcal C$,
$$[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k,\qquad H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B).$$
If the formal first-order square-root coefficient is written as $mc^2+K/(2m)$ with $K=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$, then its spin term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$, where $\mathbf S=\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma/2$. Under the coefficient convention $H_{\mathrm{mag}}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}\cdot\mathbf B$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}=g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S$, equality of the formal coefficients as a linear function of $q$ gives $g_s=2$ for the minimal tree-level term. No magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, operator square-root theorem, radiative correction, or empirical prediction is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $m>0$, smooth $A$, and the common compactly supported smooth core $\mathcal C$. Use the explicit finite Dirac matrices and the SI constants and gauge-unit conventions stated above.

[F1] [[lem-qft-example-spin-trace-completeness]]: the Hermitian Pauli/Dirac blocks satisfy $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I_4+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$ and $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$.

[F2] [[def-qft-example-data]]: $c$ is in metres per second, $\hbar$ is in joule-seconds, $q$ is in coulombs, and spatial $A_i$ is in tesla-metres.

## Proof

1.1 For $\psi\in\mathcal C$, expand $\pi_i\pi_j\psi-\pi_j\pi_i\psi$. The second derivatives and products $A_iA_j$ cancel; the remaining derivative terms are $iq\hbar(\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i)\psi=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\psi$. Smoothness of $A$ ensures each multiplication and differentiation maps $\mathcal C$ to itself. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Expand $(\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol\pi)^2=\alpha_i\alpha_j\pi_i\pi_j$. The $\delta_{ij}$ term in [F1] is $\boldsymbol\pi^2$. Its antisymmetric term is
$$\frac{i}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k[\pi_i,\pi_j] =-\frac{q\hbar}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ij\ell}\Sigma_kB_\ell =-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B,$$
because $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ij\ell}=2\delta_{k\ell}$. The cross terms with $\beta mc^2$ cancel by $\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0$, and $\beta^2=I_4$. This proves the displayed square identity on $\mathcal C$; no product outside that core is used. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 In the formal expansion parameter $t$, let $E(t)=mc^2+t\,aK+O(t^2)$ and require $E(t)^2=m^2c^4+t\,c^2K+O(t^2)$. Comparing the coefficient of $t$ gives $2mc^2aK=c^2K$, hence $a=1/(2m)$ since $m>0$. The spin part of $K/(2m)$ is $-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B/(2m)=-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The coefficient of the term linear in $q$ is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. Equating it with $-g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$ as a formal coefficient identity gives $g_s=2$, including the zero-charge specialization of that identity. This is only a formal lowest-order coefficient comparison, not an operator or empirical conclusion. [step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎
